statement: In a 4 by 4 grid, rows are numbered 1 to 4 from the top and columns 1 to 4 from the left. The squares at row 1, column 1 and row 1, column 2 are shaded. At least how many more squares must be shaded so the pattern looks the same after a quarter turn about the grid's centre?

choices.misconception: I made the pattern look the same after a half turn only, which needs just the 2 squares opposite the shaded ones.
I counted all 8 squares of the finished pattern, including the 2 that were already shaded.
I only copied the corner square to the other three corners and forgot that the second shaded square needs copies too.
I turned the pattern a quarter turn twice and shaded the new squares each time, but forgot the third quarter turn.

hints: Where does each shaded square go after one, two and three quarter turns?
For the pattern to survive a quarter turn, every shaded square must come with the three squares it lands on after one, two and three quarter turns. Track each shaded square around the grid.
The corner square lands on the other three corners. The square in row 1, column 2 lands on row 2, column 4, then row 4, column 3, then row 3, column 1.

solutions.reliable: Turn the grid clockwise a quarter turn at a time. The corner square in row 1, column 1 visits the other three corners, so 3 more squares are needed. The square in row 1, column 2 visits row 2, column 4, then row 4, column 3, then row 3, column 1, so 3 more again. These six squares are all different, so 6 further squares must be shaded, and the finished 8-square pattern does look the same after a quarter turn. The transferable idea: under quarter-turn symmetry, squares come in groups of four (apart from a centre square), so complete every group.

whyOnTest: Tests rotational symmetry: every shaded square must come with all of its images under a quarter turn, and it is easy to stop short.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
